passage: Yusuf, I heard you on the phone with your father just now. Can I tell you something from my own life? When I was about your age, my Appa retired and then just faded. He stopped reading the newspaper. He sat on the balcony till dark and barely spoke at meals. I was the one living at home, so I quietly took over: the bills, his tablets, the cooking, even reminding him to bathe. I felt I had become his parent, and I was frightened and guilty all the time, because I was angry too. My brothers in the city had no idea. One night I finally phoned them and said, "I can't do this alone." That weekend all three of us sat with Appa and said, "We love you. You don't seem yourself. Let's see Dr Rao together." He grumbled, but he went. It helped him, slowly. And it helped me more than I can say. I'm Uma, and I wish I'd called them sooner.

qa.q: Where did Uma's Appa sit till dark?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What did Uma feel while quietly taking over everything?
qa.a: Uma felt frightened and guilty, and angry too, as if Uma had become Appa's parent.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Uma?
qa.a: Phoning the brothers and saying "I can't do this alone", which led all three to speak lovingly with Appa and take him to Dr Rao.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when all three children sat with him?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed, hence the grumbling, but also loved and less alone, which is why he agreed to go.

grounding: It shows an older person recalling seeing a father withdraw, feeling role reversal, fear and guilt, and choosing to share the load with siblings and suggest a doctor.

passage: Ammi called Parveen four times before noon, as she did most days now. Had Parveen reached work? Was the gas off at home? Had Nadeem's train arrived safely? On the crowded station platform, Parveen could barely hear her over the announcements. Ammi's voice was thin and fast, and she said she hadn't slept properly since Abbu's operation. Parveen felt her chest tighten. Somewhere in the last year she had started parenting her own mother, and it frightened her. She also felt guilty for being irritated by the calls. That night she texted her brother Nadeem: "Ammi isn't okay. I've been handling it alone and I can't. Can we both talk to her on Sunday?" On Sunday, squeezed onto Ammi's bed, they held her hands. "Ammi, we love you. This much worry is hard on your health. Will you come with us to Dr Mathew?" Ammi cried, then nodded. Nadeem booked the visit; Parveen promised to come too.

qa.q: How many times did Ammi call before noon?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What two feelings did Parveen have about Ammi's calls?
qa.a: Fear at having started to parent her own mother, and guilt at feeling irritated by the calls.

qa.q: Which choice changed things, and why?
qa.a: Parveen stopped handling it alone and asked Nadeem to talk to Ammi together, so the load was shared and Ammi was gently steered to a doctor.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when both children held her hands?
qa.a: She may feel loved and seen rather than scolded, which is why she cried and then agreed to see Dr Mathew.

grounding: It shows a young woman seeing her mother constantly worried, feeling role reversal, fear and guilt, and speaking with love and her brother to suggest a doctor visit.

He'd been carrying it quietly for weeks when his friend Bilal said, "You can't hold this alone. What about your sister?" That evening Wei sat beside his father. "Ba, I love you. You've seemed very low since you retired. Can we see Dr Tan, just to check?" His father sighed but didn't refuse. Then Wei called his sister, and they split the week between them.

passage: In the waiting room of the family clinic, Tarun, twenty-four, watched his father, Sachin, fold and unfold the appointment slip. For months Papa had stopped laughing at the news, stopped his walks, stopped calling relatives. It had taken Tarun three tries to get him here. "I feel like I'm your father now," Tarun thought, and felt a pang of guilt for thinking it. He'd been scared to say anything, afraid of insulting Papa. Finally last week he'd said, "Papa, I love you. You don't seem yourself. Let's see Dr Kulkarni together." Now, while they waited, Tarun texted his sister in Delhi: "We're at the clinic. Can you call him every evening this week?" She replied at once: "Yes. Thank you for doing this."

passage:
Dear Sudha didi,
I need to talk to you about Ma. Since Papa's operation, she calls me ten times a day. She asks if I've locked the door, if I'm eating, if Papa's reports are okay. She's barely sleeping; I hear her pacing at 3 a.m.
I feel like I've become the parent, and I'm scared. I also feel guilty for getting irritated with her.
I don't want to just silently carry this. Can we talk to Ma together this weekend, lovingly, and suggest she see Dr Iyer about her worry and sleep? I'll handle the appointment. Could you take the evening calls, so she has you to talk to too?
We're in this together.
Your brother,
Hemant

qa.q: When does Hemant hear Ma pacing?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: How does Hemant feel about Ma's constant worry?
qa.a: He feels scared and guilty, like he has become the parent, and irritated at times.

qa.q: What plan does Hemant suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Talking to Ma lovingly together, suggesting a doctor for her worry and sleep, and sharing tasks with his sister rather than carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Sudha may feel worried about Ma but also grateful that her brother reached out to share the load.

grounding: Shows a young adult who sees his mother constantly worried, feels role reversal, fear and guilt, and chooses loving words, a doctor visit and sharing with his sister.

passage:
You asked what the hardest part of this year was, Sudha. Honestly? It was seeing Appa like that. I'm Ojas, the elder one, and I was always the one Appa worried about, not the other way round.
After he retired, he stopped reading the paper, stopped going for walks, sat in his chair all day. Amma was frantic, calling me every night.
Suddenly I was the parent. I was scared something was really wrong, and guilty that I lived two hours away. For weeks I just absorbed it, said nothing, lay awake.
Then one Sunday I sat next to him. "Appa, I love you. You don't seem like yourself. Can we see Dr Menon together?" He grumbled. But he went.
And then I called you. Remember? I said, "I can't do this alone." You took the Tuesday calls with Amma. That changed everything, Sudha.

qa.q: Which doctor did Ojas suggest Appa see?
qa.a: Dr Menon.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when Appa withdrew after retiring?
qa.a: Ojas felt frightened that something was really wrong and guilty about living two hours away, like the roles had reversed.

qa.q: What helped more than silently absorbing it?
qa.a: Speaking to Appa with love, suggesting a doctor visit together and sharing the load with Sudha.

qa.q: What would change if Ojas had kept absorbing everything alone?
qa.a: Ojas might have burned out, Appa might not have seen a doctor, and Sudha would never have been asked to share the Tuesday calls with Amma.

grounding: Ojas sees Appa withdrawn and Amma worried, feels role reversal, fear and guilt, and speaks with love, suggests a doctor and shares the load with a sibling.
